text: A dev or test VM that runs 24/7 is billing for hours nobody uses it. Nobody's logged in at 2 AM or on a Saturday, but by default the VM keeps running, and keeps billing, until someone stops it.

Do the math once: a week is 168 hours. A typical business week, 8 AM to 6 PM Monday through Friday, is only 50 of those hours. Running just those 50 instead of all 168 is roughly a 70% cut to that VM's compute cost, with zero change to what it can do during the workday. Across thirty dev/test VMs in a resource group, that's a real, large monthly savings — exactly the kind of waste Cost analysis would surface if you grouped spend by resource group and noticed compute that never dips on weekends.

The schedule should only touch VMs meant to follow it — production VMs serving real traffic stay untouched. A tag makes that selection explicit: Update-AzTag marks a VM with AutoShutdown = true. Anything without that tag is invisible to the scripts that follow, by design, so a script never accidentally stops something it shouldn't.

The stop script runs every weekday evening. It finds every VM tagged AutoShutdown = true and stops it with -Force, so it doesn't wait on a confirmation prompt nobody's there to answer at 6 PM. Stop-AzVM deallocates the VM — releasing the compute hardware so the per-hour charge actually stops, not just shutting down the guest OS, which would keep billing.

The matching start script runs every weekday morning, starting the same tagged VMs so a running environment is waiting when the team logs in. Neither script helps if someone has to remember to run it, so both are published as runbooks in Azure Automation, each attached to its own schedule asset — one firing at 6 PM, the other at 8 AM, every weekday, indefinitely.

Once both schedules exist, the VMs stop and start themselves with no one clicking anything. Next up: automating tag compliance checks — making sure tags like AutoShutdown, the very tag this schedule depends on, are actually present and correct across every resource, not just assumed.
